claim: Translation of aberrant mRNAs can cause ribosomes to stall, leading to collisions with trailing ribosomes.
source: Translation of aberrant mRNAs can cause ribosomes to stall, leading to collisions with trailing ribosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about ribosome behavior.

claim: Collided ribosomes are specifically recognised by ZNF598 to initiate protein and mRNA quality control pathways.
source: Collided ribosomes are specifically recognised by ZNF598 to initiate protein and mRNA quality control pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: EDF1 is a ZNF598-independent sensor of ribosome collisions.
source: Here we found using quantitative proteomics of collided ribosomes that EDF1 is a ZNF598-independent sensor of ribosome collisions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1.

claim: EDF1 stabilises GIGYF2 at collisions to inhibit translation initiation in cis via 4EHP.
source: EDF1 stabilises GIGYF2 at collisions to inhibit translation initiation in cis via 4EHP.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The GIGYF2 axis acts independently of the ZNF598 axis.
source: The GIGYF2 axis acts independently of the ZNF598 axis, but each pathway's output is more pronounced without the other.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments in ZNF598 knockout cells shown in Figures 1, 2, and 6.

claim: Each pathway's output is more pronounced without the other.
source: The GIGYF2 axis acts independently of the ZNF598 axis, but each pathway's output is more pronounced without the other.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by functional analysis in Figure 6.

claim: EDF1 is widely conserved and highly abundant.
source: We propose that the widely conserved and highly abundant EDF1 monitors the transcriptome for excessive ribosome density, then triggers a GIGYF2-mediated response to locally and temporarily reduce ribosome loading.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by abundance estimates cited in the discussion.

claim: EDF1 monitors the transcriptome for excessive ribosome density.
source: We propose that the widely conserved and highly abundant EDF1 monitors the transcriptome for excessive ribosome density, then triggers a GIGYF2-mediated response to locally and temporarily reduce ribosome loading.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: When collisions persist, translation is abandoned to initiate ZNF598-dependent quality control.
source: Only when collisions persist is translation abandoned to initiate ZNF598-dependent quality control.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model in the abstract, supported by the tiered response data.

claim: Rapidly growing cells typically produce an average of one to two proteins per ribosome per minute.
source: Rapidly growing cells typically produce an average of one to two proteins per ribosome per minute (Princiotta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: Both the amount and quality of proteins produced from a cell's transcriptome are crucial for cellular homeostasis.
source: Both the amount and quality of proteins produced from a cell's transcriptome are crucial for cellular homeostasis (Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Cells have evolved numerous mechanisms for regulating translation output.
source: Thus, cells have evolved numerous mechanisms for regulating translation output (Roux and Topisirovic, 2018) and monitoring protein quality during and after translation (Wolff et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: One of the earliest monitors of protein quality detects ribosomes that stall during translation.
source: One of the earliest monitors of protein quality detects ribosomes that stall during translation (Brandman and Hegde, 2016; Joazeiro, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: A ribosome that slows excessively can be an indicator of several potential problems including a damaged or incorrectly processed mRNA.
source: A ribosome that slows excessively can be an indicator of several potential problems including a damaged or incorrectly processed mRNA (Shoemaker and Green, 2012), amino acid or energy insufficiency (Harding et al., 2019; Inglis et al., 2019), or certain types of cellular stress (Liu et al., 2013; Shalgi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Inability to respond appropriately to ribosome stalling problems leads to disrupted protein homeostasis and disease.
source: Inability to respond appropriately to these problems leads to disrupted protein homeostasis and disease (Kapur and Ackerman, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: A common cause of ribosome stalling is a defective mRNA.
source: Because a common cause of ribosome stalling is a defective mRNA, stalled ribosome detection is linked to mRNA decay (Shoemaker and Green, 2012) and degradation of the partially synthesised protein (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010; Joazeiro, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Stalled ribosome detection is linked to mRNA decay and degradation of the partially synthesised protein.
source: Because a common cause of ribosome stalling is a defective mRNA, stalled ribosome detection is linked to mRNA decay (Shoemaker and Green, 2012) and degradation of the partially synthesised protein (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010; Joazeiro, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: There are at least two mechanisms that cells use to detect a stalled ribosome.
source: There are at least two mechanisms that cells use to detect a stalled ribosome.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and elaborated with citations.

claim: In the case of an mRNA truncated within the coding region, ribosomes stall at the 3' end with an empty A site.
source: In the specialised case of an mRNA truncated within the coding region, ribosomes stall at the 3' end with an empty A site that cannot be engaged by either elongation or termination complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The Pelota-Hbs1 complex initiates a ribosome splitting reaction for ribosomes stalled at truncated mRNAs.
source: This allows efficient engagement by the Pelota-Hbs1 complex to initiate a ribosome splitting reaction that separates the peptidyl-tRNA-60S complex from the mRNA-40S complex (Becker et al., 2011; Pisareva et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2016; Shoemaker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The 60S complex from a split ribosome is engaged by ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) factors to trigger polypeptide degradation.
source: The 60S complex is engaged by ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) factors to trigger polypeptide degradation (Shao et al., 2015), while the 40S complex engages mRNA decay pathways by still poorly-understood mechanisms (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: When a ribosome slows excessively within the coding region, its detection relies on ZNF598.
source: When a ribosome slows excessively within the coding region, its detection relies on ZNF598 (Hel2 in yeast), an E3 ubiquitin ligase whose ubiquitination of a 40S ribosomal protein (eS10 in mammals or uS10 in yeast) initiates downstream mRNA quality control (Ikeuchi et al., 2019) and protein quality control (Garzia et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: ZNF598 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: When a ribosome slows excessively within the coding region, its detection relies on ZNF598 (Hel2 in yeast), an E3 ubiquitin ligase whose ubiquitination of a 40S ribosomal protein (eS10 in mammals or uS10 in yeast) initiates downstream mRNA quality control (Ikeuchi et al., 2019) and protein quality control (Garzia et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: ZNF598 ubiquitinates eS10 in mammals or uS10 in yeast.
source: When a ribosome slows excessively within the coding region, its detection relies on ZNF598 (Hel2 in yeast), an E3 ubiquitin ligase whose ubiquitination of a 40S ribosomal protein (eS10 in mammals or uS10 in yeast) initiates downstream mRNA quality control (Ikeuchi et al., 2019) and protein quality control (Garzia et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The cue used by ZNF598 to recognise a slow ribosome is the collision that occurs when a trailing ribosome catches up.
source: The cue used by ZNF598 to recognise a slow ribosome is the collision that occurs when a trailing ribosome catches up (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The collided ribosome shows a distinctive 40S-40S interface where ZNF598/Hel2 is proposed to bind and ubiquitinate nearby target sites.
source: The collided ribosome shows a distinctive 40S-40S interface where ZNF598/Hel2 is proposed to bind and ubiquitinate nearby target sites (Ikeuchi et al., 2019; Juszkiewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The steps downstream of ZNF598 are incompletely understood.
source: The steps downstream of ZNF598 are incompletely understood and appear to involve nuclease (D'Orazio et al., 2019), a helicase complex (Hashimoto et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2017; Sitron et al., 2017), and possibly ribosome rescue factors (Tsuboi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: ZNF598-mediated 40S ubiquitination is required for downstream quality control events.
source: Although the roles and order of action of these factors is only partially resolved (Juszkiewicz et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2020), the requirement for ZNF598-mediated 40S ubiquitination (Garzia et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017) together with the specificity of ZNF598 for ribosome collisions (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018) strongly argues that the collided ribosome is a key proxy of aberrant translation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The collided ribosome is a key proxy of aberrant translation.
source: Although the roles and order of action of these factors is only partially resolved (Juszkiewicz et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2020), the requirement for ZNF598-mediated 40S ubiquitination (Garzia et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017) together with the specificity of ZNF598 for ribosome collisions (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018) strongly argues that the collided ribosome is a key proxy of aberrant translation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Collisions are an upstream event in both mRNA decay and nascent protein quality control.
source: Hence, collisions are an upstream event in both mRNA decay (Simms et al., 2017) and nascent protein quality control (Ikeuchi et al., 2019; Juszkiewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Nearly all insight into ribosome stalling and the downstream consequences comes from the analysis of model substrates where specific stalling sequences have been introduced.
source: Nearly all insight into ribosome stalling and the downstream consequences comes from the analysis of model substrates where specific stalling sequences have been introduced.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about the field.

claim: The set of substrates that ordinarily engage RQC are poorly understood.
source: However, the set of substrates that ordinarily engage RQC are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: The analysis of RNAs that crosslink to ZNF598 identified mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs.
source: The analysis of RNAs that crosslink to ZNF598 identified mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs, consistent with its engagement of translating ribosome (Garzia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The tRNA that was strongly enriched in ZNF598 crosslinking decodes the AAA codon.
source: Strikingly, the tRNA that was strongly enriched decodes the AAA codon while no specific mRNAs were enriched above others.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on cited work.

claim: Ribosomes are well established to stall during translation of poly(A) sequences.
source: This observation can be rationalised because ribosomes are well established to stall during translation of poly(A) sequences (Chandrasekaran et al., 2019) and polyadenylation is known to occur inappropriately at near-cognate sites within the coding region (Guydosh and Green, 2017; Ozsolak et al., 2010; Pelechano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Polyadenylation is known to occur inappropriately at near-cognate sites within the coding region.
source: This observation can be rationalised because ribosomes are well established to stall during translation of poly(A) sequences (Chandrasekaran et al., 2019) and polyadenylation is known to occur inappropriately at near-cognate sites within the coding region (Guydosh and Green, 2017; Ozsolak et al., 2010; Pelechano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Prematurely polyadenylated mRNAs are likely to be one physiologically relevant source of ribosome stalling, collisions, and ZNF598 engagement.
source: Thus, prematurely polyadenylated mRNAs are likely to be one physiologically relevant source of ribosome stalling, collisions, and ZNF598 engagement.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from cited work.

claim: Promiscuous triggering of quality control reactions from normal translation complexes would be detrimental.
source: While the quality control events downstream of collisions have evolved to eliminate aberrant proteins and mRNAs, promiscuous triggering of these reactions from normal translation complexes would be detrimental.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a logical inference.

claim: Reticulocytes downregulate the collision sensor ZNF598.
source: This might be why reticulocytes, which have exceptionally high ribosome densities on highly translated haemoglobin mRNAs, downregulate the collision sensor ZNF598 (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Mills et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: A detectable proportion of ribosomes in native reticulocyte polysomes are collided.
source: Indeed, a detectable proportion of ribosomes in native reticulocyte polysomes are collided as judged by their ability to engage exogenously added ZNF598 and resistance to separation by exogenously added nuclease (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Juszkiewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Most cells cannot forgo translation quality control.
source: Unlike the terminally differentiating reticulocyte with a minimal transcriptome and limited life-span, most cells cannot forgo translation quality control.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a logical inference.

claim: How cells either minimise incidental collisions or avoid promiscuous activation of quality control from them is not clear.
source: How cells either minimise incidental collisions or avoid promiscuous activation of quality control from them is not clear.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: Incidental collisions are probably not insignificant considering the wide variation in elongation rates combined with closely spaced ribosomes on heavily translated mRNAs.
source: Although the precise frequency of incidental collisions is not well established, they are probably not insignificant considering the wide variation in elongation rates (Boersma et al., 2019; Ingolia et al., 2011; Riba et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2016), combined with closely spaced ribosomes on heavily translated mRNAs (Palade, 1955).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Recent ribosome profiling experiments examining collided di-ribosomes suggest widespread collisions at numerous pause sites throughout the transcriptome.
source: Indeed, recent ribosome profiling experiments examining collided di-ribosomes suggest widespread collisions at numerous (potentially physiologic) pause sites throughout the transcriptome (Arpat et al., 2019; Han et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Quantitative proteomics identified 598 proteins in polyribosome fractions.
source: Tandem mass tag (TMT) mass spectrometry of these polyribosome fractions identified 598 proteins (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to source data.

claim: Core ribosomal proteins were tightly clustered at the origin in the mass spectrometry analysis.
source: As expected, core ribosomal proteins were seen to be tightly clustered at the origin (orange circles) providing an internal control for the comparisons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Only a handful of the 598 detected proteins were enriched on collided polysomes relative to both untreated polysomes and elongation-arrested polysomes.
source: Only a handful of the 598 detected proteins were enriched on collided polysomes relative to both untreated polysomes (x-axis) and elongation-arrested polysomes (y-axis).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ZNF598 was the most enriched collision-specific interaction partner.
source: ZNF598 was the most enriched collision-specific interaction partner consistent with prior biochemical experiments in vitro and in cells (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1A and a citation.

claim: Only EDF1 and GIGYF2 remained enriched on collided ribosomes in ZNF598 knockout cells.
source: The proteomes of globally stalled (with high-dose emetine) versus globally collided (with low-dose emetine) polysomes showed that only EDF1 and GIGYF2 remained enriched on collided ribosomes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Out of almost 600 proteins detected in polysomes, only two were identified to be enriched on collided polysomes relative to both stalled and unperturbed polysomes in both wild type and ZNF598-KO cells.
source: Thus, out of almost 600 proteins detected in polysomes, only two were identified to be enriched on collided polysomes relative to both stalled and unperturbed polysomes in both wild type and ZNF598-KO cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the mass spectrometry findings.

claim: Both EDF1 and GIGYF2 are primarily observed in non-ribosomal fractions.
source: Immunoblotting of size-fractionated cytosol showed that both EDF1 and GIGYF2 are primarily observed in non-ribosomal fractions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An estimated 5–10% of both EDF1 and GIGYF2 co-fractionated with polysomes.
source: Importantly, long exposures of the blots showed that an estimated 5–10% of both proteins co-fractionated with polysomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Figure 1C.

claim: When cells were pre-treated with low-dose emetine, the polysome-associated populations of EDF1 and GIGYF2 sharply increased to 60% and 75%, respectively.
source: When cells were pre-treated with low-dose emetine, the polysome-associated populations of EDF1 and GIGYF2 sharply increased to 60% and 75%, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Figure 1C.

claim: No appreciable population of either EDF1 or GIGYF2 was enriched in the mono-ribosome fractions.
source: Notably, no appreciable population of either protein was enriched in the mono-ribosome fractions.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Figure 1C.

claim: Parallel analysis in ZNF598 KO cells showed very similar fractionation patterns for EDF1 and GIGYF2.
source: Parallel analysis in ZNF598 KO cells showed very similar fractionation patterns: a minor polysome-associated population of EDF1 and GIGYF2 in untreated cells that increases markedly in cells containing extensive ribosome collisions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Similar results for EDF1 and GIGYF2 enrichment on collisions were seen in reticulocyte lysate.
source: Similar results were seen in reticulocyte lysate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which is naturally devoid of ZNF598 due to its downregulation during erythrocyte differentiation (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018; Mills et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to a figure supplement and citations.

claim: The binding of GIGYF2 to collided ribosomes was not via mRNA because its digestion with nuclease did not displace GIGYF2 from collided ribosomes.
source: The binding of GIGYF2 to collided ribosomes was not via mRNA because its digestion with nuclease did not displace GIGYF2 from collided ribosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In two different systems using two different methods to generate ribosome collisions, EDF1 and GIGYF2 are collision-specific ribosome interactors.
source: Thus, in two different systems using two different methods to generate ribosome collisions, EDF1 and GIGYF2 are collision-specific ribosome interactors.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the findings.

claim: GIGYF2 and EDF1 engage ribosome collisions in a ZNF598-independent manner.
source: These results corroborate the unbiased mass spectrometry analysis and establish that GIGYF2 and EDF1 engage ribosome collisions in a ZNF598-independent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Earlier studies have shown that GIGYF2 can inhibit translation initiation by recruiting the alternative cap-binding protein 4EHP.
source: Earlier studies have shown that GIGYF2 can inhibit translation initiation by recruiting the alternative cap-binding protein 4EHP (also known as EIF4E2) (Morita et al., 2012; Peter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: Recruitment of 4EHP to an mRNA allows it to outcompete the normal cap-binding protein eIF4E to prevent initiation.
source: Recruitment of 4EHP to an mRNA allows it to outcompete the normal cap-binding protein eIF4E to prevent initiation (Chapat et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: 4EHP was enriched ~1.5 fold on collided ribosomes relative to either normal translating polysomes or non-collided stalled polysomes.
source: Consistent with this idea, 4EHP was enriched ~1.5 fold on collided ribosomes relative to either normal translating polysomes or non-collided stalled polysomes (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to source data.

claim: GIGYF2 knockdown resulted in a ~2.5 fold increase in GFP output from the stalling reporter.
source: We found that GIGYF2 knockdown resulted in a ~2.5 fold increase in GFP output from the stalling reporter, but very little effect from a matched reporter lacking the stall sequence (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GIGYF2 knockdown had very little effect on a matched reporter lacking the stall sequence.
source: We found that GIGYF2 knockdown resulted in a ~2.5 fold increase in GFP output from the stalling reporter, but very little effect from a matched reporter lacking the stall sequence (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The effect of GIGYF2 knockdown could be ascribed to an effect on translation since quantitative RT-PCR showed no obvious effects on mRNA levels.
source: This effect could be ascribed to an effect on translation since quantitative RT-PCR showed no obvious effects on mRNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: A GFP-tagged protein lacking a 2A sequence showed no effect of GIGYF2 knockdown.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, a GFP-tagged protein lacking a 2A sequence showed no effect of GIGYF2 knockdown.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Figure 2B.

claim: The translation effect of GIGYF2 is substrate-specific and linked to ribosome stalling.
source: Thus, the translation effect of GIGYF2 is substrate-specific and linked to ribosome stalling.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Knockdown of 4EHP resulted in an increase in translation output selectively from the stall-containing reporter.
source: As with GIGYF2, knockdown of 4EHP also resulted in an increase in translation output selectively from the stall-containing reporter (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The effect of 4EHP was dependent on GIGYF2 because no change in translation output was seen with 4EHP knockdown in GIGYF2 KO cells.
source: Regardless, the effect of 4EHP was dependent on GIGYF2 because no change in translation output was seen with 4EHP knockdown in GIGYF2 KO cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The translational effects of GIGYF2 and 4EHP knockdown were observed in ZNF598 KO cells.
source: Consistent with GIGYF2 recruitment to collided ribosomes independently of ZNF598, the translational effects of GIGYF2 and 4EHP knockdown were observed in ZNF598 KO cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GIGYF2 represses translation initiation via 4EHP consistent with earlier studies demonstrating their interaction.
source: Considered together, these results indicate that GIGYF2 represses translation initiation via 4EHP consistent with earlier studies demonstrating their interaction (Morita et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion with a citation.

claim: GIGYF2 primarily operates in cis to inhibit translation from mRNAs to which it is recruited via collided ribosomes.
source: Because the effects are more prominent on stall-containing ribosomes that incur collisions, we further infer that GIGYF2 primarily operates in cis to inhibit translation from mRNAs to which it is recruited via collided ribosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the data.

claim: EDF1 is a highly conserved factor found throughout the eukaryotic kingdom and in archaea.
source: The other ZNF598-independent factor that we found to engage collided ribosomes is EDF1, a highly conserved factor found throughout the eukaryotic kingdom and in archaea.
evidence: This is stated in the results as established knowledge.

claim: Deletion of the EDF1 homolog (Mbf1) in yeast was recently shown to cause increased frameshifting at ribosome stall sequences.
source: Deletion of the EDF1 homolog (Mbf1) in yeast was recently shown to cause increased frameshifting at ribosome stall sequences (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: The stall sequences used in the yeast system do not detectably stall ribosomes in mammals.
source: The stall sequences used in the yeast system, certain di-codon pairs or a stem-loop, do not detectably stall ribosomes in mammals (Arthur et al., 2015; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: Mammalian ribosomes primarily stall on lengthy poly(A) sequences.
source: Instead, mammalian ribosomes primarily stall on lengthy poly(A) sequences (Arthur et al., 2015; Chandrasekaran et al., 2019; Garzia et al., 2017; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations.

claim: Poly(A) sequences that are sufficiently long to trigger a clear stall also cause extensive frameshifting.
source: Unfortunately, poly(A) sequences that are sufficiently long to trigger a clear stall, such as (KAAA)21, also cause extensive frameshifting (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: The (KAAA)12 sequence causes some stalling, but less baseline frameshifting than (KAAA)21.
source: We therefore tested a shorter poly(A) sequence [composed of (KAAA)12] that causes some stalling, but less baseline frameshifting (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: The (KAAA)12 sequence allows detectable RFP expression even for the out-of-frame constructs.
source: By contrast, the (KAAA)12 sequence inserted between GFP and RFP allows detectable RFP expression even for the out-of-frame constructs.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Relative to the RFP signal for the in-frame construct, ~7% and ~13% signal was seen for the +1 and −1 frame constructs, respectively, for (KAAA)12.
source: Relative to the RFP signal for the in-frame construct, ~7% and ~13% signal was seen for the +1 and −1 frame constructs, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon siRNA-mediated knockdown of EDF1, little if any increase in the out-of-frame signal was observed for (KAAA)12.
source: Upon siRNA-mediated knockdown of EDF1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), little if any increase in the out-of-frame signal was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The relative stalling potencies of XBP1 sequences were confirmed using in-frame versions of the reporters.
source: Using the in-frame versions, we confirmed the relative stalling potencies of these XBP1 sequences (Figure 3B) and verified that the stall-inducing variants are dependent on ZNF598 for aborting translation at the stall (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The stall-inducing XBP1 variants are dependent on ZNF598 for aborting translation at the stall.
source: Using the in-frame versions, we confirmed the relative stalling potencies of these XBP1 sequences (Figure 3B) and verified that the stall-inducing variants are dependent on ZNF598 for aborting translation at the stall (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ZNF598-dependence indicates that ribosome collisions occur effectively at the stall-inducing sequences.
source: ZNF598-dependence indicates that ribosome collisions occur effectively at the stall-inducing sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the data.

claim: The ZNF598-independence of XBP1(W256A) indicates reduced or no collisions at this sequence.
source: Conversely, the ZNF598-independence of XBP1(W256A) indicates reduced or no collisions at this sequence, providing a negative control for frameshifting experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the data.

claim: The non-stalling XBP1(W256A) reporters showed RFP signals of ~2% and ~9% in the +1 and −1 frames, respectively, relative to the in-frame construct.
source: Comparison of the three-frame set of non-stalling XBP1(W256A) reporters showed RFP signals of ~2% and ~9% in the +1 and −1 frames, respectively, relative to the in-frame construct (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The strong-stalling XBP1(S255A) constructs showed out-of-frame signals of 8% and 15% in the +1 and −1 frames, respectively.
source: Parallel analysis of the strong-stalling XBP1(S255A) constructs showed out-of-frame signals of 8% and 15% in the +1 and −1 frames, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Collisions enhance the extent of frameshifting.
source: This indicates that collisions enhance the extent of frameshifting.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Upon knockdown of EDF1, the frameshifting frequency did not change appreciably for the non-stalling XBP1(W256A) reporter.
source: Upon knockdown of EDF1, the frameshifting frequency did not change appreciably for the non-stalling XBP1(W256A) reporter but clearly increased in the −1 frame for both the medium-stalling XBP1 and strong-stalling XBP1(S255A) reporters (Figure 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Upon knockdown of EDF1, frameshifting clearly increased in the −1 frame for both the medium-stalling XBP1 and strong-stalling XBP1(S255A) reporters.
source: Upon knockdown of EDF1, the frameshifting frequency did not change appreciably for the non-stalling XBP1(W256A) reporter but clearly increased in the −1 frame for both the medium-stalling XBP1 and strong-stalling XBP1(S255A) reporters (Figure 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.
